questions.question: What is an API, and why is it needed?
questions.answer: API stands for Application Programming Interface — a set of rules that allow two software systems to communicate. APIs are needed because different systems (frontend, backend, third-party services) need a standardised, secure way to exchange data without exposing internal implementation details. Example: A food app's frontend calls a backend API to fetch restaurant menus — without knowing how the backend stores that data.

questions.question: What is AWS API Gateway and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: AWS API Gateway is a fully managed service that acts as a front door between clients and backend services. It solves the problem of exposing backend services safely and efficiently — handling authentication, request validation, throttling, routing, and monitoring. Without it, every service would need its own auth, rate limiting, and public endpoint — creating duplication and security risks.

questions.question: What are the four parts of an HTTP request?
questions.answer: Every HTTP request has four parts: (1) Method — what action to perform (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE); (2) URL — where to send the request; (3) Headers — extra metadata like authentication tokens and content type; (4) Body — the data payload, present only in POST, PUT, and PATCH requests. GET and DELETE typically have no body.

questions.question: Explain GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE with real examples.
questions.answer: GET = Read: fetch user profile data. POST = Create: register a new user account. PUT = Update/Replace: update all fields of a user profile. DELETE = Remove: delete a user account. These four map to CRUD operations — Create (POST), Read (GET), Update (PUT), Delete (DELETE). PATCH is also used for partial updates — changing just one field like an email address.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 404 and a 500 error?
questions.answer: 404 Not Found is a client-side error (4xx) — the URL path requested does not exist or has not been defined in API Gateway. It means the request was wrong, not the server. 500 Internal Server Error is a server-side error (5xx) — the request was valid but the backend crashed or threw an unhandled exception. With 4xx, fix the request. With 5xx, fix the backend.

questions.question: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
questions.answer: 401 Unauthorized means the client has not proven their identity — they are not logged in or their token is missing/invalid. 403 Forbidden means the client is identified but does not have permission to access that resource. Analogy: 401 = no ticket at all. 403 = ticket for economy trying to enter business class.

questions.question: How does API Gateway route requests to different backend services?
questions.answer: API Gateway routes requests based on the combination of resource path and HTTP method. You define resources (paths like /users, /orders) and methods (GET, POST) in API Gateway and configure each combination to point to a specific backend — a Lambda function, EC2 endpoint, or other HTTP service. When a request arrives, API Gateway matches the path and method and forwards it to the configured integration.

questions.question: What is a VPC Endpoint, and why would you use one?
questions.answer: A VPC Endpoint is a private connection between a VPC and an AWS service that keeps all traffic within the AWS network — no internet, NAT Gateway, or VPN required. You use it when you have resources in a private subnet (no internet access) that need to call AWS services like S3 or DynamoDB. Benefits: enhanced security (no internet exposure), cost savings (eliminates NAT Gateway charges), and lower latency.

questions.question: What are the two types of VPC Endpoints, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: Gateway Endpoints: support only S3 and DynamoDB, are free, and work by adding a route table entry to direct traffic through the AWS network. Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink): support most AWS services (CloudWatch, SNS, SQS, Secrets Manager, etc.), create an ENI with a private IP inside the subnet, and are charged per hour and per GB processed.

questions.question: What are the three types of API Gateway, and when do you use each?
questions.answer: REST API: full-featured, supports caching, request transformation, usage plans, WAF — use for complex enterprise APIs needing advanced capabilities. HTTP API: lightweight, up to 71% cheaper, lower latency, supports JWT auth natively — use for most standard API use cases. WebSocket API: persistent bidirectional connections — use for real-time apps like live chat, collaborative editing, live stock tickers.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to debug an API error. Walk me through your approach.
questions.answer: (Situation) A production API started returning 500 errors for 20% of requests after a deployment. (Task) I needed to identify the root cause quickly to restore service. (Action) I first checked CloudWatch logs for the Lambda function integrated with API Gateway — found an unhandled exception in the new code when the input contained null values. I checked the API Gateway CloudWatch logs to confirm the 500 originated from Lambda, not Gateway. Fixed the null check in Lambda, redeployed, and monitored for 10 minutes. (Result) Error rate dropped to 0% within 5 minutes of the fix.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would design an API for a food delivery application.
questions.answer: (Situation) Design a RESTful API for a food delivery app with users, restaurants, orders, and payments. (Task) Structure resources and methods clearly. (Action) I would create one API Gateway with these resources: /users (GET list, POST create), /users/{userId} (GET, PUT, DELETE), /restaurants (GET list, POST add), /restaurants/{id}/menu (GET), /orders (POST create order), /orders/{orderId} (GET status, PUT update), /payments (POST initiate). Each resource routes to a dedicated Lambda or microservice. Auth via Cognito JWT. (Result) Clean separation of concerns, single entry point for all clients, easy to extend.

questions.question: Your private EC2 is trying to access S3 but timing out. There is no internet access. How do you fix this?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 in a private subnet with no NAT Gateway cannot reach S3. (Task) Enable S3 access without adding internet connectivity. (Action) Create a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3 in the VPC. During creation, select the route table associated with the private subnet — this adds a route entry directing S3-bound traffic through the endpoint. No code changes needed. (Result) EC2 can now access S3 privately through the AWS backbone network. No NAT Gateway needed, free of charge.

questions.question: An API is working fine for most users but one user keeps getting 429 errors. What is happening and how do you resolve it?
questions.answer: (Situation) 429 Too Many Requests for one specific user. (Task) Allow legitimate users access while stopping abuse. (Action) 429 means API Gateway throttled that client. For REST API: create a usage plan defining per-client rate limits (e.g., 100 RPS, 10,000 requests/day), issue API keys to clients, associate the usage plan with the API key. The abusive client's key gets throttled while others continue normally. (Result) Fair usage enforced per client without affecting others.

questions.question: How would you secure an API Gateway endpoint so only authenticated users can call it?
questions.answer: (Situation) A REST API needs authentication for all endpoints. (Task) Implement auth without building it from scratch. (Action) Three options depending on use case: (1) Cognito Authorizer — users sign in to Cognito User Pool and get a JWT; API Gateway validates the JWT for every request. (2) Lambda Authorizer — custom Lambda validates tokens (OAuth, custom) and returns an IAM policy. (3) IAM Authorization — for internal service-to-service calls using AWS credentials. For a consumer app, Cognito is the most common choice. (Result) Only requests with valid tokens reach the backend.

questions.question: A company wants to reduce AWS costs. Their private EC2s make millions of calls to DynamoDB daily via NAT Gateway. What would you recommend?
questions.answer: (Situation) High NAT Gateway costs due to EC2-to-DynamoDB traffic. (Task) Reduce cost while maintaining functionality. (Action) Replace the NAT Gateway path with a Gateway VPC Endpoint for DynamoDB. Gateway Endpoints are free — no hourly charge, no per-GB charge. The endpoint routes DynamoDB traffic directly through the AWS backbone. Update the route table to include the endpoint route. (Result) Eliminated NAT Gateway data processing charges for DynamoDB traffic, potentially saving hundreds of dollars monthly depending on volume.

questions.question: How does API Gateway handle a request end-to-end?
questions.answer: (Situation) Client clicks Submit Order. (Task) Trace the request flow. (Action) (1) Client sends HTTP request with method, URL, headers, and body to API Gateway endpoint. (2) API Gateway checks authentication — is the token valid? (3) Validates the request format. (4) Checks throttle limits — is this client within their rate limit? (5) Matches the resource (path) and method to find the backend integration. (6) Forwards request to backend (Lambda/EC2). (7) Backend processes and returns response. (8) API Gateway returns response to client with appropriate status code. (Result) Clean, secure, monitored request lifecycle.

questions.question: You need to expose 10 different microservices through one URL. How do you design this with API Gateway?
questions.answer: (Situation) 10 microservices, each a separate Lambda or EC2. (Task) Single URL, clean routing. (Action) Create one API Gateway. Define one resource (path) per service — /users, /orders, /payments, /inventory, etc. Under each resource, define the needed methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). Each method integrates with the corresponding backend service. Deploy to a stage (prod). Clients use one base URL and differentiate services by path. (Result) Clean microservices facade, easy to add/modify services independently.

questions.question: Explain the difference between an Interface Endpoint and a Gateway Endpoint with a use case for each.
questions.answer: Gateway Endpoint: Free, supports only S3 and DynamoDB, works via route table modification. Use case: A data processing EC2 in a private subnet reads raw files from S3 and writes results to DynamoDB — Gateway Endpoints for both eliminate NAT Gateway dependency at zero cost. Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink): Paid (per hour + per GB), supports most AWS services, creates an ENI with private IP in the subnet. Use case: A security-sensitive private application needs to call CloudWatch for logging and Secrets Manager for credentials — Interface Endpoints enable this without any internet traffic.

questions.question: When would you choose REST API over HTTP API in API Gateway?
questions.answer: Choose REST API when you need: (1) API-level response caching — REST API supports cache TTL settings to reduce backend load; (2) Request/response transformation — modify headers or body before forwarding; (3) Per-client usage plans and API keys for fine-grained throttling; (4) AWS WAF integration for security filtering; (5) Edge-optimized endpoints via CloudFront. Choose HTTP API for everything else — it is simpler, cheaper (71% less), and faster. Most new APIs should start with HTTP API unless a specific REST-only feature is needed.

questions.question: How would you design a real-time bidirectional communication system using API Gateway?
questions.answer: Use WebSocket API in API Gateway. Architecture: (1) Clients connect to the WebSocket API endpoint — a persistent connection is established. (2) API Gateway maintains a connection registry; each connection gets a unique connectionId. (3) When a client sends a message, it triggers a Lambda function (onMessage route). (4) Lambda can push messages back to connected clients using the API Gateway Management API with the connectionId. (5) For broadcasting (e.g., chat room), use DynamoDB to store active connectionIds and loop through them. (Result) True real-time bidirectional communication — server can push updates without the client asking.

questions.question: What happens to VPC Endpoint traffic at the network level? How is it different from public internet traffic?
questions.answer: Public internet traffic from a private EC2 goes: EC2 → NAT Gateway (private subnet route table) → Internet Gateway → public internet → AWS service endpoint (public IP). This traffic leaves the AWS network, incurs NAT Gateway charges, and is visible on the public internet. VPC Endpoint traffic stays entirely within the AWS backbone network. For Gateway Endpoints, the route table entry redirects traffic for S3/DynamoDB prefixes directly through the AWS network fabric — never touching the internet. For Interface Endpoints, an ENI in the subnet receives the traffic and forwards it through PrivateLink within the AWS backbone. Result: Private, faster, cheaper, and more secure.

questions.question: How does API Gateway integrate with Lambda for a serverless REST API? Explain Proxy vs Non-Proxy integration.
questions.answer: Lambda Proxy Integration: API Gateway passes the entire request (method, path, headers, query params, body) to Lambda as a single event object. Lambda must return a properly formatted response with statusCode, headers, and body. Simple and flexible — Lambda has full control. Lambda Non-Proxy Integration: API Gateway uses mapping templates to transform the request before passing to Lambda, and transforms Lambda's response before returning to client. More complex but allows API Gateway to reshape data formats without changing Lambda code. For most use cases, Proxy integration is preferred for simplicity.

questions.question: A company needs to allow a partner's application running in a different AWS account to access their internal service privately. How would you architect this?
questions.answer: Use AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints) for cross-account private connectivity. Architecture: (1) Company A creates a VPC Endpoint Service backed by a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of their internal service. (2) They whitelist Company B's AWS account. (3) Company B creates an Interface Endpoint in their VPC pointing to Company A's Endpoint Service. (4) An ENI is created in Company B's subnet with a private IP. (5) All traffic between Company B's application and Company A's service flows privately through PrivateLink — never over the internet, no VPC peering needed. (Result) Secure, private, scalable cross-account service access.

questions.question: An API Gateway returns 502 Bad Gateway. How is this different from 500, and what would you check?
questions.answer: 500 Internal Server Error means the Lambda function ran but threw an unhandled exception. 502 Bad Gateway means API Gateway received an invalid or malformed response from the backend — Lambda ran but returned something API Gateway couldn't parse. Common causes of 502: (1) Lambda returned a response without the required statusCode field (with Proxy Integration). (2) Lambda returned invalid JSON in the body field. (3) Lambda timed out and returned no response (which API Gateway interprets as malformed). Steps to debug: Check CloudWatch Logs for the Lambda function — look at the actual return value. Verify the response format matches API Gateway Proxy Integration requirements: {'statusCode': 200, 'body': json.dumps({...})}.
